judge_persona: Independent Judge B: pragmatic hackathon evaluator who scores strictly against each PDF's written criteria and weights, rewards complete, reproducible, demonstrable work over ambition, and discounts anything that exists only on slides. Assumes a student team strong in Python/Node/React/backend with AI/ML integration exposure, no specialist domain engineers, no paid APIs, no guaranteed hardware.

candidates.main_failure_risk: Commoditisation: C-MAPSS is a heavily tutorialised benchmark, so a bare FD001 + random forest + Streamlit build looks like every other submission. The team only wins if it covers all four subsets, reports honest per-subset RMSE/NASA-score with sensible RUL clipping, and shows a genuinely closed loop (new data -> retrain -> model registry -> agent -> work order) with no manual steps. Model-performance over-claiming (test-set leakage, unclipped RUL) is the most common way to lose the 15% model criterion and the 20% demo criterion.

rubric.rationale: Problem is crisply defined in the PDF with a public dataset; a backend team can restate objectives, imbalance handling and the closed-loop intent accurately.
data -> features -> model -> agent -> work order is a natural software pipeline; the team's systems background makes a clean component diagram with interfaces straightforward.
Rolling-window features, normalisation per operating condition (FD002/FD004), RUL label clipping are well documented; team can propose a sound approach but will not have novel insight.

Needs justified choice of anomaly detector (e.g. Isolation Forest / reconstruction error) plus RUL regressor (GBM vs LSTM/1D-CNN) with awareness of imbalance and operating regimes. AI/ML 'exposure' rather than depth caps this; judges will probe why a method was chosen.
MLflow tracking + retrain trigger + rule-based severity thresholds is squarely backend engineering; a clear decision table for the Triage Agent is easy to specify.
Full marks require a design that scales across FD001-FD004 (multi-regime, multiple fault modes). Feasible but must be planned from Round 1, not bolted on.
Low weight, well within the team's reach with a structured deck.
Single-command, end-to-end run on a public CSV dataset with open-source tools is exactly what a backend team does well; highest-confidence criterion in the whole exercise.
Reproducible, tested feature pipeline (pandas, fixed seeds, schema checks) is achievable; robustness across subsets takes extra care.

Credible results with correctly interpreted metrics (RMSE, NASA asymmetric score, per-subset) are attainable, but stronger ML teams will post better numbers; honesty about FD002/FD004 difficulty matters more than leaderboard chasing.
Live MLflow run, model version promotion and a demo retraining run on appended data are demonstrable without any special resources.
Deterministic rules on RUL + anomaly score -> severity -> work-order JSON/ticket with human-exception path; easy to unit-test and show reliably.
Requires actually running and reporting on all four subsets; feasible on a laptop but doubles the validation work.
20% weight on articulating trade-offs and improvements; team can demo well but must defend ML choices against reviewers who know C-MAPSS intimately.

candidates.what_a_winning_submission_shows: One command (make run / docker compose up) that ingests all four C-MAPSS subsets, builds rolling features, trains an anomaly detector and an RUL model with per-subset RMSE and NASA score reported honestly, logs everything to MLflow with versioned models, serves a Streamlit monitoring view, and has a rule-based Triage Agent that emits a work order for a unit crossing an RUL/severity threshold while routing ambiguous cases to a human queue; then a live retraining run on newly appended cycles that promotes a new model version. Plus a short, candid trade-off section (why GBM vs LSTM, clipping choice, drift handling).

candidates.main_failure_risk: Domain credibility: the rubric puts 35% on Technical feasibility + Engineering quality and 15% on measurable, repeatable evidence. A software team without a battery/EE member will build a plausible-looking web simulator whose thermal and ageing assumptions a Tata Elxsi battery engineer can dismantle in two questions. Unlike the other cases, a polished UI does not compensate for wrong physics.

rubric.rationale: Requires defining an application, requirements and operating conditions for a cell group/module; achievable from datasheets and literature but will read as textbook rather than practitioner understanding.
A student-facing design-trade-off explorer is genuinely desirable and the team can pitch it well; this is the one criterion their product sense helps.

Scoping to a small series/parallel cell group with an equivalent-circuit + lumped thermal model (or PyBaMM) is feasible and safe, but the team cannot validate against real cells and must convince judges the simplifications are appropriate.
Sound calculations and system-interaction understanding (I^2R heating, cooling, derating, ageing propagation) are outside the team's demonstrated background; highest risk of visible errors.
Simulation results are repeatable, but 'measurable' evidence without any low-voltage experiment or reference data leaves the model unvalidated; expect partial credit only.
Comparing options with traceability from requirement -> assumption -> result and automatic interface-conflict flagging is a software-native idea the team can realise.
Reusable platform story is easy to tell; moderate credit.

candidates.what_a_winning_submission_shows: A tightly scoped module (e.g. 4s2p 21700 cells) modelled with an openly documented ECM + lumped thermal model (ideally PyBaMM-backed), three configurations compared against a baseline on usable energy, peak temperature, charge time, mass and cost, with every parameter traced to a datasheet, explicit safety limits that trigger violations in the UI, and an honest limitations page. Winning teams in this case will likely also have a small bench measurement; this team almost certainly will not.

candidates.main_failure_risk: Depth of Linux networking: real tc/HTB/fq_codel/CAKE shaping, netem impairment, flow-feature classification without payload inspection and a reset-run-measure-report harness is a lot of unfamiliar systems work for a Python/Node team, and it must run on a Linux host with root. If the testbed is flaky or the setup guide does not reproduce on the evaluator's machine, every one of the five measurable criteria collapses at once.

rubric.criterion: Accuracy of classification and link estimation
rubric.rationale: Flow-metadata classifier (packet size, inter-arrival, ports, DNS/SNI hints) with confidence and a user-correction path is buildable, but accuracy on realistic mixed traffic without a labelled dataset is hard to prove; link estimation via active probing is doable but noisy.

rubric.criterion: Reduction in interactive latency, jitter and packet loss
rubric.rationale: In a netem/namespace testbed, moving from FIFO to fq_codel/CAKE + bulk-class shaping produces large, easily measured latency-under-load improvements; this is the most demonstrable criterion.
HTB class guarantees with a floor for bulk traffic plus Jain's fairness index on the dashboard is standard and verifiable.
Reacting to a 100->20 Mbps drop without oscillation requires hysteresis and careful tuning; achievable but easy to get wrong and judges will look for stable convergence plots.

rubric.criterion: CPU overhead, reproducibility and clarity of results
rubric.rationale: Backend discipline (scripts, pinned versions, docker/namespaces, auto-generated reports) plays to the team's strength; CPU overhead of a Python controller is low at home-link scale.

candidates.what_a_winning_submission_shows: A single script that spins up network namespaces or VMs, applies netem impairments, runs the three PDF scenarios (ISO download vs video call, WAN drop, 3 TVs + gaming) under baseline and controller, and emits a report with latency/jitter/loss/throughput/queue-depth/fairness plots and a classifier confusion matrix with confidence; a REST endpoint to set a temporary 'prioritise my call' intent with automatic expiry and rollback; a deterministic-rules baseline against any ML classifier; licenses, fictitious secrets, emulation labels and a known-limitations section exactly as the PDF requests.

candidates.main_failure_risk: Regulatory credibility and no ground truth: HLS reviewers will test whether the compliance checker encodes ISO 15223-1 symbols, UDI structure and MDR/FDA label elements correctly. A team with no regulatory background and no real label corpus will either hard-code a shallow rule set or lean on a local LLM whose 'compliance' judgments are unverifiable, and 'Accuracy & validation approach' becomes a hand-wave. The breadth of the ten listed approaches also tempts slideware over a working slice.

rubric.rationale: The PDF supplies the full process map and pain points; a process map + automation opportunity matrix can be assembled from the document itself.
Requires working knowledge of EU MDR Annex I Ch.III, 21 CFR 801, ISO 15223-1, UDI-DI/PI format; the team can read the references but will make mistakes an RA judge spots.

rubric.criterion: Innovation ideas considering Label Design using AI
rubric.rationale: GenAI drafting + rule-based checks + CV redline diff is an obvious but credible combination the team can prototype with local models.
Workflow engine, approval states, document parsing, OCR/diff pipeline: core backend engineering; this is where the team outbuilds typical submissions.
Eighteen-step process; a demonstrable slice covering change impact -> content -> check -> redline -> approval -> release is feasible, but full coverage will be partly narrated.
No public labelled dataset; the team would have to synthesise labels and seeded defects, which judges may accept as methodology but not as evidence of real accuracy.
Immutable audit log, element-to-requirement links and change-order lineage are database/backend problems the team can nail.

candidates.what_a_winning_submission_shows: A working slice: a product-change event triggers an impact engine that lists affected labels/markets, a GenAI assistant drafts content with every element linked to a requirement ID, a deterministic checker validates UDI check digits, mandatory symbols and required elements against a machine-readable rule set, a CV diff produces a redline between artwork versions, and an approval workflow writes an audit trail; evaluated on a synthetic corpus with seeded defects and reported precision/recall. Winning teams will additionally cite regulations precisely and include a validation plan a QA engineer recognises.

candidates.main_failure_risk: The edge constraint: 2 GB RAM, 2 ARM cores, <2 s responses with no cloud. Without a Raspberry Pi or ARM board the team will measure on an x86 laptop or a cgroup-limited container, and automotive reviewers will discount those numbers. Data Integration (CAN, SOME/IP, VHAL, QNX logs) will be mostly simulated CAN plus architecture text, which is thin against a criterion that explicitly asks for multiple protocols.

rubric.rationale: Simulation -> ingestion -> time-series store -> retrieval -> SLM -> UI with safety-domain isolation is a diagram a systems team draws well; completeness of the hardware side will be weaker.

A quantised 0.5-1.5B model via llama.cpp doing intent routing + text-to-SQL/templated analytics can answer the PDF's five example queries, but free-form accuracy at that size is fragile; needs a small query eval set to prove it.
python-can/vcan and DBC decoding are achievable; SOME/IP, Android VHAL and QNX logs are outside reach and will be paper-only.
Event search, trend and anomaly queries over DuckDB/SQLite with rolling statistics and a simple cause-chain ('events in the N minutes before warning X') is a backend strength.
Memory footprint and latency can be reported, but credibility depends on real ARM hardware or at least a documented qemu/Graviton run; scalability story will be qualitative.
Local-only processing, no network egress, encrypted store and read-only bridge from the vehicle domain are easy to implement and demonstrate.
Hybrid 'small model for intent + deterministic analytics' is practical and defensible; value for service engineers is easy to articulate.

candidates.what_a_winning_submission_shows: A simulated vehicle (recorded/synthetic CAN logs with injected faults such as battery over-temperature and ADAS disengagements) streamed into a local store retaining weeks of data, a llama.cpp-served small model that routes questions to validated analytics functions or constrained SQL and explains results, measured p50/p95 latency and RSS on a Raspberry Pi 4/5 (or a clearly labelled ARM VM) under 2 GB, a query accuracy table on 30-50 test questions, and an architecture that isolates the AI domain from safety-critical ECUs. Teams that actually show the hardware numbers will beat teams with better demos on a laptop.

rationale: Case 1 is the clear first choice. It is the only case with a prescribed public dataset, open-source tool suggestions, and two weighted rubrics in which roughly 70% of Round 2 marks (working pipeline, data engineering, MLOps, agent behaviour, demo) reward exactly what a backend-strong team delivers reliably: a reproducible end-to-end system. Its weakness is differentiation, not feasibility, and the fix (all four subsets, honest metrics, real retraining loop) is within reach. Case 3 is second because all five criteria are objectively measurable, every deliverable is software, and a scripted baseline-vs-optimised testbed lets a working prototype score on evidence rather than slides; it ranks below Case 1 only because Linux tc/netem/classifier work is unfamiliar territory with a long deliverable list and a single point of failure (the testbed). Case 5 is third: the team's model-integration skill fits well and privacy/search criteria are easy, but Edge Performance and Data Integration are hard to earn without ARM hardware or automotive protocol experience, and the unweighted, partly design-oriented criteria mean more depends on presentation. Case 4 is fourth: the platform/traceability parts suit the team, but two of seven criteria hinge on regulatory expertise and there is no ground-truth corpus, so accuracy claims are unverifiable; it still beats Case 2 because it is software-shaped. Case 2 is last: 50% of its weight (feasibility, engineering quality, prototype evidence) rests on battery physics the team cannot validate, and the judges will be domain engineers. Scores are deliberately spread (8.0 / 7.0 / 6.3 / 5.6 / 5.3) to reflect that the gap between Case 1 and the rest is primarily about verifiability by judges, which this persona weights heavily.
tie_breaker_information_needed: The only near-tie is Case 3 vs Case 5 (7.0 vs 6.3). It resolves on three facts: (a) whether any teammate has a Linux machine with root (or comfort with VMs/namespaces) and prior exposure to tc/iptables, which de-risks Case 3; (b) whether the team owns or can borrow a Raspberry Pi 4/5 (8 GB is fine, cgroup-limited to 2 GB) to produce real ARM latency numbers, which lifts Case 5's Edge Performance from 5.5 toward 7; (c) the competition format (number of rounds, live demo vs recorded video, judge composition), since Case 3's objective metrics favour a live reproducible run while Case 5 favours a polished recorded demo. For Case 1 vs the field no tie-breaker is needed; the only thing that would change it is evidence that the team has a specialist (battery/EE for Case 2, regulatory affairs for Case 4, automotive embedded for Case 5).
